title: Test planning: the test plan, release and iteration planning, entry and exit criteria
body:
# Chapter 5 in one line
Chapter 5 is about **managing** the test activities: planning them, steering them by risk, watching and correcting them, keeping their work products under control and handling the defects they find. It carries **9 of the 40** exam questions, and three of the eight K3 slots (estimation, prioritisation, defect report).

This chapter comes in three lessons for §5.1: this one (the plan, release and iteration planning, entry and exit criteria), then estimation and prioritisation, then the test pyramid and the testing quadrants.

# FL-5.1.1 (K2): what a test plan is for
A **test plan** describes the objectives, resources and processes for a test project. Its purposes:
- it documents the **means and the schedule** for reaching the test objectives;
- it helps make sure the testing done will meet the established criteria;
- it is a **means of communication** with team members and other stakeholders;
- it shows that testing will follow the existing **test policy** and **test strategy** (or explains why it deviates).

Planning is also a way of *thinking ahead*: writing the plan forces the team to face risks, schedules, people, tools, costs and effort before they turn into surprises.

Typical content of a test plan:
- **Context of testing:** scope, test objectives, constraints, test basis
- **Assumptions and constraints** of the test project
- **Stakeholders:** roles, responsibilities, relevance to testing, hiring and training needs
- **Communication:** forms and frequency, documentation templates
- **Risk register:** product risks and project risks
- **Test approach:** test levels, test types, test techniques, test deliverables, entry and exit criteria, independence of testing, metrics to collect, test data and test environment requirements, deviations from the organisation's test practices
- **Budget and schedule**

A test plan is not written once and frozen: it is **updated** as the project goes on and feedback comes in. Bigger projects may have a master test plan plus plans per test level or test type.

Game example: the plan for a new co-op raid lists the scope (the raid, not the whole game), the risk register (server load on launch night is a product risk; the only network tester going on leave is a project risk), the test levels and types, which console kits are needed, and when testing must finish before certification submission.

**Exam trap:** "the test plan is the detailed list of test cases". Wrong: test cases come from test analysis, design and implementation. The plan describes objectives, approach, resources, schedule and risks.

# FL-5.1.2 (K1): the tester in release and iteration planning
In iterative development there are two planning horizons.

**Release planning** looks ahead to the release of the product. It defines and re-defines the **product backlog**, and may refine large user stories into smaller ones. It is the basis for the test approach and the test plan across all iterations. Testers contribute by:
- writing **testable user stories and acceptance criteria**
- taking part in **project and quality risk analyses**
- **estimating test effort** for the user stories
- determining the **test approach**
- **planning the testing** for the release

**Iteration planning** looks ahead to the end of one iteration and is about the **iteration backlog**. Testers contribute by:
- taking part in the **detailed risk analysis** of user stories
- determining the **testability** of user stories
- **breaking user stories down into tasks**, especially testing tasks
- **estimating test effort** for all testing tasks
- identifying and refining the **functional and non-functional aspects** of the test object

**Exam trap:** release vs iteration. The whole product backlog, the release-wide test approach and plan → release planning. Testability of individual stories, breaking stories into tasks, the iteration backlog → iteration planning. Estimating test effort and risk analysis appear in both (risk analysis in release planning, the *detailed* one per story in iteration planning).

# FL-5.1.3 (K2): entry criteria and exit criteria
**Entry criteria** are the **preconditions** for starting an activity. If they are not met, the activity is likely to be harder, slower, more costly and riskier. Typical entry criteria:
- **availability of resources:** people, tools, environments, test data, budget, time
- **availability of testware:** test basis, testable requirements, user stories, test cases
- **initial quality level of the test object:** for example, all smoke tests have passed

**Exit criteria** define what must be **achieved** to declare an activity complete. Typical exit criteria:
- **measures of thoroughness:** achieved coverage, number of unresolved defects, defect density, number of failed test cases
- **binary yes/no criteria:** planned tests have been run, static testing has been done, all defects found are reported, all regression tests are automated

**Running out of time or budget** can also be a valid exit criterion: testing may stop if the stakeholders have reviewed and **accepted the risk** of going live without further testing.

Each test level, and each activity, can have its own entry and exit criteria; they are defined in the test plan.

In Agile:
- exit criteria are often called the **Definition of Done** (the team's objective metrics for a releasable item);
- the entry criteria a user story must meet before development or testing starts are called the **Definition of Ready**.

Game example (different from the questions you will see):
- Entry criteria for system testing of a new map: the build installs on the test kits, the map loads, the smoke test passed, the map's design document is approved.
- Exit criteria: 100% of the planned map tests run, no open defects of the highest severity, 90% of the map's requirements covered.

**Exam trap:** the time-test. A criterion about *starting* ("the build has passed the smoke test", "the test environment is available") is an **entry** criterion. A criterion about *finishing* ("80% requirements coverage reached", "no open critical defects") is an **exit** criterion. Same wording can sit on either side if it is about a *different* activity: "component testing is complete" is an exit criterion for component testing and an entry criterion for the next level.

**Exam trap:** "Definition of Ready = exit criteria". The wrong way round: Ready is the entry side, Done is the exit side.

# Unity connections
- A Unity Cloud Build that fails its automated smoke scene is a classic unmet entry criterion for the QA pass.
- "Certification checklist passed and no open crash defects" is an exit criterion before a console submission.
- Sprint planning in Jira is iteration planning: that is where you split "As a player I can trade items" into testing tasks and estimate them.

title: Test effort estimation and test case prioritisation
body:
# Why estimate, and why prioritise
**Test effort estimation** predicts the amount of test-related work needed to meet the test objectives. An estimate is always based on **assumptions** and is affected by **estimation error**: estimates for small tasks are usually more accurate than for large ones, so a big task is often broken down into smaller ones first.

**Test case prioritisation** decides the order in which test cases run, so the most important ones run first if time runs out.

Both are K3: you will **calculate** an estimate or **work out** an execution order. Work it on paper, then compare with the options.

# FL-5.1.4 (K3): four estimation techniques
The syllabus names four techniques in two groups.

**Metrics-based** (from data):
- **Estimation based on ratios:** use ratios from *previous* projects in the organisation. Example: in the studio's last three DLCs, test effort was 1 person-day for every 4 person-days of development (ratio 4:1). The new DLC needs 480 person-days of development, so test effort ≈ 480 ÷ 4 = **120 person-days**.
- **Extrapolation:** take measurements as early as possible in the *current* project and extend them. Example: the first three sprints needed 22, 26 and 24 person-days of testing. The average is (22 + 26 + 24) ÷ 3 = 72 ÷ 3 = **24 person-days**, so the next sprint is estimated at 24.

**Expert-based** (from people's judgement):
- **Wideband Delphi:** experts estimate **in isolation**. The results are collected; experts whose estimates are far outside the agreed range explain them; then everyone estimates again, alone, until a **consensus** is reached. **Planning Poker** is an Agile variant, with estimates on cards (often Fibonacci-style numbers).
- **Three-point estimation:** experts give three estimates: the most **optimistic** (a), the most **likely** (m) and the most **pessimistic** (b).

The three-point estimate is a weighted average, **E = (a + 4m + b) ÷ 6**, and its spread is the standard deviation, **SD = (b − a) ÷ 6**.

Worked example: testing a new save-game system. a = 4, m = 7, b = 16 person-days.
- E = (4 + 4 × 7 + 16) ÷ 6 = (4 + 28 + 16) ÷ 6 = 48 ÷ 6 = **8 person-days**
- SD = (16 − 4) ÷ 6 = 12 ÷ 6 = **2**
- So the estimate is **8 ± 2 person-days**: between 6 and 10.

**Exam trap:** "three-point = the average of the three numbers". Wrong: (4 + 7 + 16) ÷ 3 = 9, not 8. The most likely value counts **four times**, and the sum is divided by **6**.

**Exam trap:** ratios vs extrapolation. Ratios come from *earlier projects*; extrapolation comes from *early measurements in this project*. Both are metrics-based.

**Exam trap:** Wideband Delphi is not "the team agrees on a number in one meeting". Each round is done **alone**, and the rounds repeat until the estimates converge.

# FL-5.1.5 (K3): three prioritisation strategies
- **Risk-based prioritisation:** the order follows the results of **risk analysis**: tests for the highest risks run first.
- **Coverage-based prioritisation:** the order follows **coverage** (code coverage, requirements coverage): the test with the highest coverage runs first. In **additional coverage-based prioritisation**, the first test is the one with the highest coverage, and each next test is the one that adds the most coverage **not yet achieved**.
- **Requirements-based prioritisation:** the order follows the **priorities of the requirements** traced to the tests; **stakeholders** set those priorities. The most important requirements are tested first.

Ideally tests run in priority order. But two things can change the order:
- **Dependencies:** if a high-priority test depends on a lower-priority one, the lower-priority one must run **first**.
- **Resources:** tools, environments or people that are only available in a certain time window.

Worked example: dependencies (1 = highest priority).

| Test | Priority | Depends on |
|---|---|---|
| T1 | 5 | none |
| T2 | 1 | T4 |
| T3 | 2 | none |
| T4 | 4 | none |
| T5 | 3 | T2 |

Rule: take the **highest-priority test not yet run**. If it depends on tests that have not run, run those **first, right before it**. Repeat.
1. T2 is the top priority but needs T4, so **T4** runs first, then **T2**.
2. Next highest: **T3** (2), no dependencies.
3. Next: **T5** (3); it needed T2, which has run.
4. Last: **T1** (5). T4 has already run.

Order: **T4, T2, T3, T5, T1**. The plain priority order T2, T3, T5, T4, T1 is impossible: T2 cannot run before T4.

Worked example: additional coverage. Five requirements R1–R5.
- TA covers R1, R2, R3 · TB covers R3, R4 · TC covers R4, R5 · TD covers R1
1. Highest coverage: **TA** (3 requirements). Covered: R1, R2, R3.
2. What each adds: TB adds R4 (1), TC adds R4 and R5 (2), TD adds nothing. → **TC**. Now all five are covered.
3. TB and TD add nothing new; they follow in any order.

Order: **TA, TC**, then TB and TD. Plain coverage-based (no "additional") would put TB and TC level after TA (2 each), so the word *additional* matters.

**Exam trap:** "the highest-priority test always runs first". Not when it depends on another test: the dependency runs first even if its own priority is low.

**Exam trap:** risk-based vs requirements-based. If the order comes from *likelihood and impact*, it is risk-based; if it comes from *stakeholder priorities of requirements*, it is requirements-based.

# Unity connections
- Planning Poker in sprint planning is Wideband Delphi in Agile form.
- "Last season's three patches took 15% of dev time to test" is the data behind ratio estimation.
- A smoke scene that loads every level is a typical dependency: nothing else runs until it passes.

title: The test pyramid and the testing quadrants
body:
# Two models, two different questions
- The **test pyramid** answers: *how many tests of each granularity should we automate?*
- The **testing quadrants** answer: *which kinds of tests do we need, and what is each one for?*

Both come up in Agile and DevOps contexts, but on the exam they are separate LOs.

# FL-5.1.6 (K1): the test pyramid
The **test pyramid** is a model showing that different tests can have different **granularity**. It supports the team in **test automation** and in **test effort allocation**: it shows that different goals are supported by different levels of automated tests.

Each layer is a group of tests. **The higher the layer:**
- the lower the test **granularity** (each test checks a bigger piece of functionality)
- the lower the test **isolation**
- the lower the test **execution speed** (slower tests)
- the **higher the cost**

So:
- **Bottom:** small, isolated, fast tests, each checking a small piece of functionality. You need **many** of them for reasonable coverage.
- **Top:** complex, high-level **end-to-end** tests, slow, each checking a big piece of functionality. You need only **a few**.

The number and names of the layers vary. The original model has *unit*, *service* and *UI* tests; another common version has *unit (component)*, *integration (component integration)* and *end-to-end* tests.

Game example: hundreds of Edit Mode tests on damage formulas (bottom), dozens of tests that run the matchmaking service against a fake server (middle), a handful of automated playthroughs from the title screen to the first boss (top).

**Exam trap:** "the top of the pyramid has the most tests because it is closest to the user". The wrong way round: the top has the **fewest**, slowest and most expensive tests.

**Exam trap:** "the pyramid shows the order in which test levels are executed". It shows how many tests of each granularity to have, not a sequence.

# FL-5.1.7 (K2): the testing quadrants
The **testing quadrants** (from Brian Marick) group **test levels** with the appropriate **test types, activities, test techniques and work products** in Agile development. They help test management make sure that **all appropriate test types and test levels** are included, and that some test types belong more to certain levels. They are also a way to explain the kinds of tests to stakeholders.

Two axes:
- **Business facing** vs **technology facing**
- **Support the team** (guide development) vs **critique the product** (measure its behaviour against expectations)

The four quadrants:

| | Support the team | Critique the product |
|---|---|---|
| Business facing | Q2 | Q3 |
| Technology facing | Q1 | Q4 |

- **Q1: technology facing, support the team.** **Component tests** and **component integration tests**. They should be **automated** and part of the **CI** process.
- **Q2: business facing, support the team.** **Functional tests, examples, user story tests, user experience prototypes, API testing** and **simulations**. They check the **acceptance criteria**; manual or automated.
- **Q3: business facing, critique the product.** **Exploratory testing, usability testing, user acceptance testing.** User-oriented and often **manual**.
- **Q4: technology facing, critique the product.** **Smoke tests** and **non-functional tests** (except usability). Often **automated**.

How to place a test: ask two questions.
1. Is it expressed in the language of the **business** (players, designers, the product owner) or of the **technology** (code, components, infrastructure)?
2. Does it help the team **build** the right thing as they go (support), or does it **judge** the finished behaviour (critique)?

Game examples (not the ones in the questions):
- A unit test on the inventory's `AddItem()` → Q1
- A Given/When/Then test for the story "a player can gift a skin to a friend" → Q2
- A playtest where new players try the tutorial while you watch → Q3 (usability)
- A soak test with 5,000 bots on the servers for 12 hours → Q4 (non-functional)

**Exam trap:** usability. It is non-functional, but it sits in **Q3**, not Q4: Q4 is "non-functional *except usability*".

**Exam trap:** "Q1 tests critique the product". No: component tests **support the team**; they guide development.

**Exam trap:** API testing feels technical, but the syllabus puts it in **Q2** (business facing, support the team), next to functional tests and simulations.

# Unity connections
- The Unity Test Framework's Edit Mode tests are the base of your pyramid and live in Q1.
- A frame-time budget check in the CI pipeline is a Q4 test.
- A closed beta with real players is Q3 (user acceptance testing).

title: Risk management
body:
# Risk management in one line
Organisations face internal and external factors that make it uncertain whether they will reach their objectives. **Risk management** raises the chance of reaching them, improves product quality and builds stakeholders' confidence. Its main activities are **risk analysis** (identification and assessment) and **risk control** (mitigation and monitoring). Testing chosen, prioritised and managed by risk is called **risk-based testing**.

# FL-5.2.1 (K1): risk, likelihood, impact, risk level
A **risk** is a potential event, hazard, threat or situation whose occurrence causes an adverse effect. A risk has two attributes:
- **risk likelihood:** the probability that it happens (more than 0 and less than 1)
- **risk impact:** the harm or consequences if it happens

Together they express the **risk level**: the higher the risk level, the more important it is to treat it.

Quantitative example: on scales of 1 to 5, a risk with likelihood 4 and impact 3 has level 4 × 3 = **12**; one with likelihood 2 and impact 5 has level 2 × 5 = **10**. The first is treated first, even though its impact is lower.

Qualitative example (a **risk matrix**): likelihood *high* and impact *medium* → level *high*; likelihood *low* and impact *low* → level *low*.

**Exam trap:** "risk level = impact". Wrong: it needs **both** likelihood and impact. A catastrophic but nearly impossible event can have a lower risk level than a moderate, very likely one.

**Exam trap:** a likelihood of 1 (certain) is not a risk any more: it is an issue that is happening. A likelihood of 0 is no risk at all.

# FL-5.2.2 (K2): project risks and product risks
**Project risks** are about the **management and control of the project**:
- **organisational issues:** delays in work product deliveries, inaccurate estimates, cost-cutting
- **people issues:** insufficient skills, conflicts, communication problems, shortage of staff
- **technical issues:** scope creep, poor tool support
- **supplier issues:** a third party fails to deliver, a supporting company goes bankrupt

If they happen, project risks affect the **schedule, budget or scope**, and so the project's ability to reach its objectives.

**Product risks** are about the **quality characteristics of the product** (the ISO 25010 model): missing or wrong functionality, incorrect calculations, runtime errors, poor architecture, inefficient algorithms, inadequate response time, poor user experience, security vulnerabilities.

If they happen, product risks can lead to: user dissatisfaction; loss of revenue, trust or reputation; damage to third parties; high maintenance costs and an overloaded help desk; criminal penalties; in extreme cases physical damage, injury or even death.

How to tell them apart: ask "**if it happens, what is hurt first?**" The project (time, money, scope, people) → project risk. The product as players use it (it does the wrong thing, or does it badly) → product risk.

Game examples:
- The external localisation vendor may deliver the Japanese text late → **project** (supplier).
- The only shader programmer may leave before launch → **project** (people).
- The leaderboard may show wrong rankings when two scores tie → **product** (incorrect calculation).
- Loading a save on an older phone may take over 30 seconds → **product** (performance).

**Exam trap:** "a risk in the test environment is a product risk because it is technical". Poor tool support or a late test environment threatens the **project** (schedule), not the product's quality characteristics.

# FL-5.2.3 (K2): how product risk analysis shapes testing
The goal of **product risk analysis** is awareness of product risk, so that test effort is focused where it **minimises the residual level of product risk**. Ideally it starts **early** in the SDLC.

It has two parts:
- **Risk identification:** building a thorough list of risks, with techniques such as brainstorming, workshops, interviews or cause-effect diagrams.
- **Risk assessment:** categorising the risks, determining their likelihood, impact and level, prioritising them and proposing ways to handle them. Categorising helps, because risks in the same category can often be mitigated in a similar way. The assessment can be **quantitative** (likelihood × impact), **qualitative** (a risk matrix), or a mix.

Product risk analysis can influence the **thoroughness and scope** of testing. Its results are used to:
- determine the **scope** of testing
- determine the particular **test levels** and propose the **test types** to perform
- determine the **test techniques** to use and the **coverage** to reach
- **estimate the test effort** for each task
- **prioritise testing** to find the critical defects as early as possible
- decide whether activities **in addition to testing** could reduce the risk

Game example: the analysis rates "in-game purchases charged twice" as the highest risk. So: payment flows get decision-table tests with full coverage, a security test type is added, they run first, and the team adds an extra code review of the payment module.

**Exam trap:** "risk analysis decides which defects to fix". No: it shapes *testing* (scope, levels, types, techniques, coverage, effort, order). Deciding which defects to fix is defect management.

# FL-5.2.4 (K2): responses to analysed product risks
**Product risk control** is every measure taken in response to identified and assessed product risks. It has two parts:
- **Risk mitigation:** carrying out the actions proposed in the assessment to **reduce the risk level**.
- **Risk monitoring:** checking that the mitigation actions are **effective**, getting more information to improve the assessment, and spotting **emerging risks**.

Once a risk is analysed, there are several **response options**:
- **risk mitigation by testing**
- **risk acceptance** (decide to live with it)
- **risk transfer** (move it to someone else, e.g. an insurer or a supplier contract)
- a **contingency plan** (prepare what to do if it happens)

Actions that mitigate product risks **by testing**:
- choose testers with the **right experience and skills** for the type of risk
- apply the right **level of independence** of testing
- carry out **reviews** and **static analysis**
- apply the right **test techniques** and **coverage levels**
- apply the right **test types** for the quality characteristics at risk
- perform **dynamic testing**, including **regression testing**

Game examples:
- Accessibility risk in the menus → bring in a tester experienced with screen readers (skills).
- The anti-cheat module is high risk → have it tested by a separate security team (independence).
- The studio buys insurance against server outage losses → transfer.
- A tiny visual glitch on one old GPU, rated very low → acceptance.
- A rollback build is prepared in case the day-one patch breaks saves → contingency plan.

**Exam trap:** "mitigation = making the risk impossible". Mitigation **reduces** the risk level; testing cannot remove all risk.

**Exam trap:** monitoring vs mitigation. *Doing* the actions = mitigation; *checking that they work and watching for new risks* = monitoring.

# Unity connections
- A crash-reporting dashboard after a soft launch is risk monitoring: it shows whether the mitigation worked and reveals new risks.
- A risk workshop with design, code and QA before alpha is risk identification.
- Choosing to run the full regression suite only on the platform with the highest crash risk is risk-based prioritisation.

title: Test monitoring, control, completion and reporting
body:
# Monitoring, control and completion
- **Test monitoring** *gathers* information about testing. It is used to assess progress and to measure whether the exit criteria, or the testing tasks tied to them, are met (for example, the coverage targets for product risks, requirements or acceptance criteria).
- **Test control** *uses* that information to give guidance and take **corrective actions**, called **control directives**.
- **Test completion** collects data from finished test activities to consolidate experience, testware and other relevant information. It happens at project milestones: a test level is complete, an Agile iteration ends, a test project is finished or cancelled, software is released, a maintenance release is complete.

Examples of control directives:
- reprioritising tests when an identified risk becomes an issue
- re-evaluating whether a test item meets the entry or exit criteria after rework
- adjusting the test schedule because the test environment was delivered late
- adding new resources when and where they are needed

**Exam trap:** monitoring vs control. "We measured that only 40% of tests have run" = monitoring. "So we move two testers onto the payment tests" = control.

# FL-5.3.1 (K1): metrics used in testing
Test metrics show progress against the planned schedule and budget, the current quality of the test object, and how effective the testing is. Common groups:
- **Project progress metrics:** task completion, resource usage, test effort
- **Test progress metrics:** test case implementation progress, test environment preparation progress, number of test cases run / not run, passed / failed, test execution time
- **Product quality metrics:** availability, response time, mean time to failure
- **Defect metrics:** number and priorities of defects found and fixed, **defect density**, **defect detection percentage**
- **Risk metrics:** residual risk level
- **Coverage metrics:** requirements coverage, code coverage
- **Cost metrics:** cost of testing, organisational cost of quality

Game examples: "312 of 400 test cases run, 20 failed" (test progress); "the matchmaking server's mean time to failure is 9 days" (product quality); "4 defects per 1,000 lines in the AI module" (defect density, a defect metric).

**Exam trap:** "mean time to failure is a defect metric". It is a **product quality** metric: it describes how the product behaves, not the defects found.

# FL-5.3.2 (K2): test reports
Test reporting **summarises and communicates** test information during and after testing.

**Test progress reports** support the ongoing **control** of testing. They must give enough information to change the test schedule, resources or test plan when the work deviates from the plan or circumstances change. They are produced **regularly** (daily, weekly…) during monitoring and control. Typical content:
- the **test period**
- **test progress** (ahead of or behind schedule), including any notable deviations
- **impediments** to testing and their **workarounds**
- **test metrics**
- **new and changed risks** in the period
- the **testing planned for the next period**

**Test completion reports** summarise a specific stage of testing (a test level, a test cycle, an iteration) and can feed later testing. They are prepared during **test completion**, when a project, test level or test type is finished and, ideally, its exit criteria are met. They use the progress reports and other data. Typical content:
- a **test summary**
- an evaluation of **testing and product quality** against the original **test plan** (test objectives and exit criteria)
- **deviations from the test plan** (schedule, duration, effort)
- testing **impediments and workarounds**
- **test metrics** based on the progress reports
- **unmitigated risks** and **defects not fixed**
- **lessons learned** relevant to testing

**Audience:** different audiences need different information, and this affects the **formality** and **frequency** of reporting. Reporting to people in the same team is usually frequent and informal; reporting on a finished project follows a template and happens once. ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119-3 has templates (it calls progress reports **test status reports**).

How to tell them apart: does it look **forward** ("planned for next period", to steer the work) → progress report. Does it look **back** on a finished stage ("lessons learned", "defects not fixed", "evaluation against the exit criteria") → completion report.

**Exam trap:** "lessons learned" belong to the **completion** report, and "testing planned for the next period" to the **progress** report.

# FL-5.3.3 (K2): ways to communicate test status
The best way to communicate test status depends on test management concerns, the organisation's test strategy, regulatory standards or, in self-organising teams, the team itself. Options:
- **verbal** communication with team members and other stakeholders
- **dashboards:** CI/CD dashboards, task boards, burn-down charts
- **electronic channels:** email, chat
- **online documentation**
- **formal test reports** (§5.3.2)

One or more can be used together. **More formal** communication may suit **distributed teams**, where face-to-face talk is not always possible because of distance or time zones. Different stakeholders want different information, so the communication should be **tailored** to them.

Game example: the QA lead in Montreal and the developers in Seoul share almost no working hours, so status goes into a written daily summary and a shared dashboard rather than a stand-up.

**Exam trap:** "a formal test report is always the best way". No single option is always best: it depends on the context and the audience.

# Unity connections
- A Unity Cloud Build or Jenkins dashboard showing the last nightly test run is a CI/CD dashboard.
- The release candidate's sign-off document for the publisher is a test completion report.
- A Jira burn-down chart for the sprint's test tasks is a dashboard.

title: Configuration management
body:
# FL-5.4.1 (K2): how configuration management supports testing
**Configuration management (CM)** gives discipline for **identifying, controlling and tracking** work products as **configuration items**. In testing, those work products include test plans, test strategies, test conditions, test cases, test scripts, test results, test logs and test reports.

For a **complex configuration item** (for example a **test environment**), CM records the items it is made of, their **relationships** and their **versions**.

**Baselines:**
- When a configuration item is approved for testing, it becomes a **baseline**.
- A baseline can only be changed through a **formal change control process**.
- CM keeps a record of changed configuration items when a new baseline is created.
- It is possible to **revert to a previous baseline** to **reproduce earlier test results**.

To support testing properly, CM makes sure that:
- **all configuration items, including test items** (the individual parts of the test object), are **uniquely identified**, **version controlled**, **tracked for changes** and **related to other configuration items**, so **traceability** can be kept throughout the test process;
- all identified documentation and software items are **referenced unambiguously** in the testware.

**Continuous integration, continuous delivery, continuous deployment** and their testing are usually built into an automated **DevOps pipeline**, which normally includes **automated CM**.

Game example: a player reports that saves corrupt on build 1.4.2 on one console. Because the build, the console firmware, the test scripts and the test data are all versioned and linked, QA restores exactly that baseline, reruns the test cases that passed at the time, and reproduces the failure.

**Why this matters for testers:**
- you can say exactly **which version** of the test object a result belongs to;
- a **defect report** can name the exact build and environment;
- you can **reproduce** an old result;
- you know which **tests** belong to which **version** of a requirement.

**Exam trap:** "configuration management = the version control system". Version control is part of it, but CM also covers identification, baselines, change control, relationships between items and traceability.

**Exam trap:** "configuration management is only for code". The syllabus lists testware (plans, cases, scripts, results, logs, reports) and test environments as configuration items too.

**Exam trap:** "a baseline can be updated by anyone who needs a change". No: only through **formal change control**.

# Unity connections
- Git (or Plastic SCM / Unity Version Control) with tagged release builds gives you baselines you can go back to.
- An environment record such as "build 1.4.2 + firmware 9.03 + test data set v7" is CM of a complex configuration item.
- Addressable asset bundles with version labels let you tie a test result to exact content.

title: Defect management and defect reports
body:
# Defect management
One major objective of testing is to find defects, so an organisation needs an established **defect management** process. Not everything reported is a real defect: an **anomaly** may turn out to be a real defect or something else, such as a **false positive** or a **change request**. That is settled while handling the report.

The process has a **workflow** for each anomaly from **discovery to closure**, plus rules for classifying them. The workflow typically:
1. **logs** the reported anomaly
2. **analyses and classifies** it
3. **decides** on a response: fix it, or keep it as it is
4. **closes** the defect report

All stakeholders involved must follow the process. Defects found in **static testing** (especially static analysis) should be handled in a similar way.

# What defect reports are for
- to give the people responsible for handling and resolving the defect **enough information to resolve it**
- to give a way of **tracking the quality** of the work product
- to give **ideas for improving** the development and test process

# FL-5.5.1 (K3): what goes into a defect report
A defect report logged during **dynamic testing** typically contains:
- a **unique identifier**
- a **title** with a short summary of the anomaly
- the **date** it was observed, the **issuing organisation** and the **author**, including their **role**
- identification of the **test object** and the **test environment**
- the **context** of the defect: the test case being run, the test activity, the SDLC phase, and other relevant information such as the test technique, checklist or test data used
- a **description of the failure** that allows **reproduction and resolution**: the **steps** that detected the anomaly, plus relevant **test logs, database dumps, screenshots or recordings**
- **expected results** and **actual results**
- the **severity** of the defect: its degree of **impact** on the interests of stakeholders or on the requirements
- the **priority** to fix
- the **status**: for example open, deferred, duplicate, waiting to be fixed, awaiting confirmation testing, re-opened, closed, rejected
- **references**, for example to the test case

Defect management tools can fill in some of these automatically (identifier, date, author, status). ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119-3 has templates (it calls defect reports **incident reports**).

# Severity vs priority (drill this)
- **Severity** = the **impact** of the defect when it occurs: how much damage it does to the stakeholders' interests or the requirements. A crash, data loss or a security hole is high severity, **however rarely it happens**.
- **Priority** = how **urgently** it should be fixed: a **business** decision, weighed with frequency, deadlines, visibility, cost and the release plan. In most teams the product owner or the triage meeting sets or confirms it; the tester proposes.

They are **independent**. All four combinations exist:

| | High priority | Low priority |
|---|---|---|
| High severity | the game crashes on the title screen for everyone | a crash only when a player renames a guild 500 times in one session |
| Low severity | the studio's name is misspelt on the store page | a one-pixel gap in a rarely seen credits screen |

**Exam trap:** "severity = how often it happens". Wrong: frequency is not severity. A rare crash is still **high severity**; its rarity may make it **low priority**.

**Exam trap:** "the tester decides the priority". The tester records severity and may suggest a priority, but priority is a **business** call.

**Exam trap:** "the store-page typo is low priority because it is cosmetic". Cosmetic means **low severity**; because every customer sees it before buying, it is **high priority**.

# Writing a good report (the K3 part)
On the exam you choose the **best** report, or spot the **missing** item. Check, in this order:
1. Can a developer **reproduce** it? (exact steps, test data, environment, build)
2. Are **expected** and **actual** results both there, and different?
3. Are **severity** and **priority** set, and set sensibly?
4. Is it **factual and neutral**? (no blame, no guesses at the cause stated as fact)
5. Is there **one** defect per report, with a clear **title**?

Worked example. A weak report: "Inventory broken, fix ASAP!!" A good report:
- **Title:** Stack of 99 potions becomes 0 after dropping 1 item (build 0.9.3, PC)
- **Environment:** build 0.9.3, Windows 11, test save "inv_full_07"
- **Steps:** 1. Load the save. 2. Open the inventory. 3. Drop one Health Potion from the stack of 99.
- **Expected:** 98 Health Potions remain. **Actual:** the stack shows 0 and disappears.
- **Severity:** high (loss of player items) · **Priority:** high (common action in every session)
- **Context:** test case INV-14, system testing, EP partition "full stack"
- **Attachments:** screen recording, player log

**Exam trap:** "the defect report should state the root cause". The tester reports the **failure** (what was observed); finding the defect and its root cause is the developer's debugging.

**Exam trap:** defect reports are born in **test execution** (when a failure is observed), not in test completion. Completion only collects the ones still open.

# Unity connections
- Attach the Player.log or Editor.log and a Unity Recorder clip: that is the "test logs, screenshots or recordings" item.
- Name the build number from Unity Cloud Build and the platform: test object and test environment.
- Jira's "Rejected" and "Duplicate" statuses match the syllabus statuses.
